intro: You already move your voice up ↗ and down ↘ for lists, question tags and feelings. Now you use it at work: to sound doubtful, surprised or polite, to correct someone with one strong word (I said TUESday, not THURSday), and to present in clear chunks with short pauses. The recordings are read in a calm, natural voice, so you add the melody: say every example out loud and exaggerate a little.
teachingNotes: Builds on b1-pron-rhythm-intonation (arrows ↗ up, ↘ down, → flat; statements and wh-questions usually fall, yes/no questions usually rise; lists; falling tag = sure, rising tag = really asking; a wide pitch range for surprise, flat and low = bored, slow low fall = annoyed, sarcasm like 'Oh, perfect. ↘') and b2-pron-connected-speech (elision, assimilation, weak forms, gonna/wanna/gotta). Recap in a line; don't re-teach. New here: the fall-rise ↘↗ for doubt and a hidden 'but', polite requests and offers, contrastive stress, and chunking with pauses when presenting. Describe melody with arrows and plain Indonesian (nada naik, turun, turun lalu naik). No IPA and no tone-unit terms except 'fall-rise', explained the first time (the voice goes down and then up again, often on one slow, stretched word).

Attitude: the same word can carry different attitudes. Really?! ↗ (fast, a wide jump from low to very high) = surprised; Really…? ↘↗ (slow, down then up) = doubtful, 'I don't really believe that' (Indonesian 'Masa sih…?'); Really. → (flat, low) = bored. The fall-rise also signals a hidden 'but' (The plan is good… ↘↗ = but there's a problem; Maybe… ↘↗ = I'm not sure). Repeating what you heard with statement word order and a big rise shows surprise (You finished it already? ↗). Polite requests and offers (Could you…? Can you…? Would you like…? Can I get you…?): start fairly high and finish with a gentle rise; a low, flat voice with a quick fall sounds impatient or like an order, even with could you or please. Wh-questions still usually fall, but start higher and fall gently. Node common error: flat intonation everywhere, so Really? sounds bored. Indonesian trap: politeness carried by words (tolong, mohon, Pak/Bu, a soft 'ya') while the voice stays flat; in English the melody carries much of the politeness. Sarcasm only as a note: recognise it (Thanks a lot. ↘ said flat and low), don't use it at work, and remember it doesn't survive in writing.

Contrastive stress: normally the strongest stress falls on the last content word (The meeting's on THURSday). To correct or contrast, move the strongest stress to the word that is different and keep the rest low and quick: No, I said TUESday, not THURSday; It's MY bag, not YOURS. Small words that are normally weak (my, your, I, she, not, did) become strong when they carry the contrast: say this is why it seems to break the B1 rule. Stress the word's normal stressed syllable (TUES-day, ba-NA-na, BAN-dung). Meaning changes with the stressed word (I didn't say she stole it: I = someone else said it; SAY = I only thought it; SHE = someone else stole it; STOLE = maybe she borrowed it; IT = she stole something else). Indonesian trap: Indonesian marks contrast with words (bukan … tapi …, yang as in 'Saya yang bayar', -lah, kok); English does it mostly with the voice, so a flat English correction gets missed. Node common error: equal stress on every word ('I said Tuesday, not Thursday'). Correcting politely = a strong contrast word plus a friendly voice (Sorry, I think it's on TUESday).

Chunking: a chunk (thought group) = a group of words that belong together, said as one unit, with a short pause after it: Last year | our sales | rose by ten percent. Pause at commas and full stops, after a time or place phrase at the start, after a long subject, and before but, because, so. Never pause inside a group that belongs together: a/the/my + noun (the | report ✗), a preposition + its noun (in | Bandung ✗), a number + its word (ten | percent ✗). Each chunk has one main stress, usually its last content word; the voice tends to stay up or level at the end of a chunk when more is coming and falls at the end of the sentence (like a list). A short silent pause sounds more confident than 'eee…' or 'um'. Node common error and Indonesian trap: reading a slide fast in one long breath (nerves), or pausing only when you run out of air, in the middle of a group. Long sentences can often be chunked in more than one good way: test only clear cases (a pause that splits a group, or the obvious pause after an opening time phrase).

Audio limits: every recording is read once by one natural voice. It does NOT demonstrate a fall-rise, exaggerated surprise, contrastive stress on demand or exact pauses. Listening questions only test what a natural reading gives (what was asked, which detail is different); intonation, stress placement and pausing are tested in text, with arrows, CAPITALS for the stressed word and | for pauses. Read-aloud English (tiles, examples, listen) is written in normal spelling without capitals or | marks; the glosses and notes carry the markings. If the learner asks to hear the difference, describe it (start low, jump high; slow, down then up) and ask them to say it aloud and exaggerate.

Grammar scope: A0–B1 grammar (present and past tenses, present perfect, will and going to, can/could/would for requests and offers, first and second conditionals, present/past simple passive). No third conditional, wish or past modals. British and American speakers use the same basic patterns; the fall-rise for doubt and polite reservation is especially common in British English. Don't teach tone-unit theory (tonic syllable, pre-head), high rising terminal or regional melodies.

keyPoints.title: Doubt, surprise and politeness in your voice
keyPoints.explanation: The same words can show different attitudes. A fast, wide jump up (Really?! ↗) = surprised. Slow, down and then up again (Really…? ↘↗, the fall-rise) = doubtful, or 'yes, but…'. In polite requests and offers, start higher and finish with a gentle rise (Could you send me the file? ↗); a low, flat voice with a quick fall can sound impatient, even with please.

examples.id: Masa? Kamu dapat kontraknya? (terkejut: lompatan naik yang besar ↗)
Masa sih? Aku nggak terlalu yakin. (ragu: pelan, turun lalu naik ↘↗)

examples.en: Could you send me the file?
examples.id: Bisa tolong kirim filenya? (sopan: mulai agak tinggi, naik pelan di akhir ↗)

id.title: Ragu, terkejut dan sopan lewat suaramu
id.explanation: Kata-kata yang sama bisa menunjukkan sikap yang berbeda. Lompatan naik yang cepat dan lebar (Really?! ↗) = terkejut. Pelan, turun lalu naik lagi (Really…? ↘↗, nada turun-naik atau fall-rise) = ragu, atau 'iya, tapi…'. Dalam permintaan dan tawaran yang sopan, mulai agak tinggi dan akhiri dengan naik yang pelan (Could you send me the file? ↗); suara rendah dan datar yang turun cepat bisa terdengar tidak sabar, walaupun pakai please.

keyPoints.title: Stress the word that corrects or contrasts
keyPoints.explanation: To correct someone or compare two things, make the word that is different the strongest and keep the rest low: I said TUESday, not THURSday. Even small words like my, your or I become strong when they carry the contrast: It's MY bag, not YOURS. Move the stress and the meaning changes.

examples.en: No, I said Tuesday, not Thursday.
examples.id: Bukan, aku bilang Selasa, bukan Kamis. (TUESday … THURSday)

examples.en: Hey, that's my bag, not yours!
examples.id: Hei, itu tasku, bukan tasmu! (MY … YOURS)

id.title: Tekan kata yang mengoreksi atau membandingkan
id.explanation: Untuk mengoreksi orang atau membandingkan dua hal, buat kata yang berbeda itu paling kuat dan sisanya tetap rendah: I said TUESday, not THURSday. Bahkan kata kecil seperti my, your atau I jadi kuat kalau kata itulah yang membawa perbedaannya: It's MY bag, not YOURS. Pindahkan tekanannya, maka artinya ikut berubah.

keyPoints.title: Present in chunks, with short pauses
keyPoints.explanation: When you present, say the words that belong together as one chunk and pause briefly between chunks: Last year | our sales | rose by ten percent. Pause after a time phrase at the start, after a long subject and before but or because. Don't pause inside a group like the report or ten percent. A short silence sounds more confident than 'eee…'.

examples.en: Last year, our sales rose by ten percent.
examples.id: Tahun lalu, penjualan kami naik sepuluh persen. (Last year | our sales | rose by ten percent)

examples.en: Our new app is fast, but it uses a lot of data.
examples.id: Aplikasi baru kami cepat, tapi memakai banyak kuota. (Our new app is fast | but it uses a lot of data)

id.title: Presentasi dalam potongan, dengan jeda singkat
id.explanation: Saat presentasi, ucapkan kata-kata yang satu kelompok sebagai satu potongan (chunk) dan beri jeda singkat di antara potongan: Last year | our sales | rose by ten percent. Beri jeda setelah keterangan waktu di awal, setelah subjek yang panjang, dan sebelum but atau because. Jangan berhenti di tengah kelompok seperti the report atau ten percent. Diam sebentar terdengar lebih percaya diri daripada 'eee…'.

guidedPractice.prompt: Her manager asks Sari: 'Will the project be ready on Friday?' Sari answers 'Maybe…' slowly, and her voice goes down and then up ↘↗. Is she sure or not sure? Write sure or not sure.
guidedPractice.hint: A slow fall-rise ↘↗ shows doubt, or a hidden 'but…'.

guidedPractice.prompt: Your friend says: 'I've just won a trip to Japan!' You're very surprised and happy for her. Does your 'Really?' jump up, go down and then up, or stay flat? Write up, down-up or flat.
guidedPractice.hint: Surprise is fast, with a wide jump from low to very high ↗.

guidedPractice.prompt: Budi asks: 'Is the presentation at two?' It's at four. You answer: 'No, it's at four.' Which word do you stress most? Write it.
guidedPractice.hint: Stress the word that corrects the mistake: two → FOUR.

guidedPractice.prompt: Rina thinks the blue folder is Dimas's. Dimas says: 'That's your folder, not mine.' Which two words does he stress? Write them.
guidedPractice.hint: The contrast is between the owners, so the small words your and mine become strong.

guidedPractice.prompt: A presenter says: 'Last year our profit grew by ten percent.' Where should she NOT pause: between 'year' and 'our', or between 'ten' and 'percent'?
guidedPractice.hint: A number and its word belong together: never split ten | percent.

independentPractice.prompt: Your colleague asks: 'Your flight to Medan is on Monday, right?' It's on Sunday. Write a short answer and put the word you stress in CAPITALS.
independentPractice.hint: Only the day is wrong, so only the day gets the strong stress: SUNday.

independentPractice.prompt: Split this slide sentence into three chunks with |: 'Last month our app had fifty thousand new users.'
expected: last month | our app | had fifty thousand new users
independentPractice.hint: Pause after the time phrase at the start and after the subject; keep fifty thousand new users together.

assessment.prompt: In a meeting, Budi says: 'The new app will be ready next week.' Bu Ani answers 'Really…?' slowly, and her voice goes down and then up again ↘↗. How does she feel about Budi's news? Write surprised, doubtful or bored.
assessment.rubric: Correct: doubtful (a slow fall-rise ↘↗ on Really means 'I don't really believe that', like Indonesian 'Masa sih…?'). 'sarcastic' = 40 (close, but sarcasm is a flat, low voice on a positive word). 'surprised' = 0 (surprise is a fast, wide jump up ↗). 'bored' = 0 (bored is flat and low →).

assessment.prompt: Sari asks a colleague: 'Could you check my slides before the meeting?' She says it in a low, flat voice that drops quickly at the end. How can this sound to her colleague? Write friendly or impatient.
assessment.rubric: Correct: impatient (a low, flat voice with a quick fall makes a request sound like an order, even with polite words like could you; a voice that starts higher and rises gently ↗ sounds friendly). 'rude' or 'bossy' = 100 (the same idea). 'friendly' = 0 (the error this lesson targets: thinking the polite words are enough).

assessment.prompt: Budi says: 'I didn't say Rina LOST the files.' (LOST is said with extra stress.) What does he mean? Write A, B or C. A: Someone else lost the files, not Rina. B: Rina did something else with the files, for example she deleted them. C: Someone else said it, not Budi.
assessment.rubric: Correct: B (the stressed word is the part being corrected: not lost, but something else she did). A = 0 (that needs extra stress on RINA). C = 0 (that needs extra stress on I).

assessment.prompt: Pak Hasan thinks Dimas sent the sales report to the client. In fact, Sari sent it. Sari tells him: 'I sent the report.' Which word does she stress most? Write the word.
assessment.rubric: Correct: I (the contrast is the person: Sari, not Dimas; Indonesian would say 'Saya yang kirim'). 'sent' = 20 (that would contrast sending with something else, like writing). 'report' = 0 (that would mean she sent the report and not something else). 'sari' = 50 (right idea, but the word in her sentence is I).

assessment.prompt: Listen to Rina's question. The training is in room twelve on the third floor. You answer: 'No, it's in room twelve on the third floor.' Which one word do you stress most? Write it.
assessment.listen: Is the training in room twelve on the second floor?
assessment.rubric: Correct: third (Rina asked about the second floor; room twelve is right, so only the floor number is corrected: …on the THIRD floor). 'twelve' = 0 (the room number she said was right). 'floor' = 0 (floor isn't the part that's different). 'second' = 0 (that's the mistake, not the correction).

assessment.prompt: A presenter has three versions of the same slide sentence, with | for the pauses. Which one is chunked clearly? Write A, B or C. A: This year our | team in Bandung doubled | its sales. B: This year | our team in Bandung | doubled its sales. C: This | year our team | in Bandung doubled its | sales.
assessment.rubric: Correct: B (time phrase | subject | the rest: no group is split). A = 0 (it splits our | team and doubled | its sales). C = 0 (it pauses in random places, splitting This | year and its | sales, as if the speaker runs out of air).

assessment.prompt: Dimas wants one short pause in this sentence on his slide: 'In the second half of the year our team opened three new offices.' After which word is the best place for the pause? Write the word.
assessment.rubric: Correct: year (the opening time phrase In the second half of the year is one chunk; then our team opened three new offices). 'team' = 30 (a pause after the subject is possible, but with only one pause the time phrase is the clear boundary). 'half', 'three' or 'new' = 0 (they split a group that belongs together).

material.title: Doubtful or surprised? Same word, different tune

blocks.text:
Quick recap: statements and wh-questions usually go **down** ↘, yes/no questions usually go **up** ↗, and a **wide pitch range** (how far your voice travels from low to high) shows feelings: a big jump up = surprised, flat and low → = bored. Now one more tune, and more attitudes.

**The fall-rise ↘↗**: the voice goes **down and then up again**, often on one slow, stretched word. It says 'I'm not sure', or 'yes, **but**…':
- *Really…? ↘↗* (slow) = 'I don't really believe that.' Like Indonesian *Masa sih…?*
- *Maybe… ↘↗* = 'maybe, but I'm not sure.'
- *The plan is good… ↘↗* = 'it's good, **but** there's a problem.' The listener waits for the *but*.

**Surprise** is different: fast, with a **wide jump** from low to very high: *Really?! ↗* Like *Hah? Masa?!* You can also show surprise by repeating what you heard as a question, with normal statement word order and a big rise: *You finished it already? ↗* *Two hundred people? ↗*

So one word can carry three attitudes:
- *Really?! ↗* fast, big jump = **surprised**
- *Really…? ↘↗* slow, down then up = **doubtful**
- *Really. →* flat and low = **bored** (not interested)

**The Indonesian trap:** a flat, Indonesian-style melody makes every *Really?* sound bored, and the listener can't tell whether you're surprised or doubtful. Let your voice move more than feels natural.

These are tendencies, not strict laws: people and regions vary, and the fall-rise is especially common in British English.

id.text:
Ulasan singkat: kalimat biasa dan wh-question biasanya **turun** ↘, pertanyaan ya/tidak biasanya **naik** ↗, dan **rentang nada yang lebar** (seberapa jauh suaramu bergerak dari rendah ke tinggi) menunjukkan perasaan: lompatan naik yang besar = terkejut, datar dan rendah → = bosan. Sekarang satu nada baru, dan lebih banyak sikap.

**Nada turun-naik ↘↗ (fall-rise)**: suaranya **turun lalu naik lagi**, sering pada satu kata yang diucapkan pelan dan panjang. Artinya 'aku nggak yakin', atau 'iya, **tapi**…':
- *Really…? ↘↗* (pelan) = 'Aku nggak terlalu percaya.' Seperti *Masa sih…?*
- *Maybe… ↘↗* = 'mungkin, tapi aku belum yakin.'
- *The plan is good… ↘↗* = 'bagus, **tapi** ada masalah.' Pendengar menunggu *but*-nya.

**Terkejut** itu beda: cepat, dengan **lompatan lebar** dari rendah ke sangat tinggi: *Really?! ↗* Seperti *Hah? Masa?!* Kamu juga bisa menunjukkan terkejut dengan mengulang yang kamu dengar sebagai pertanyaan, dengan urutan kata kalimat biasa dan nada naik yang besar: *You finished it already? ↗* *Two hundred people? ↗*

Jadi satu kata bisa membawa tiga sikap:
- *Really?! ↗* cepat, lompatan besar = **terkejut**
- *Really…? ↘↗* pelan, turun lalu naik = **ragu**
- *Really. →* datar dan rendah = **bosan** (tidak tertarik)

**Jebakan untuk orang Indonesia:** melodi datar ala bahasa Indonesia membuat setiap *Really?* terdengar bosan, dan pendengar tidak bisa tahu apakah kamu terkejut atau ragu. Biarkan suaramu bergerak lebih banyak dari yang terasa wajar.

Ini kecenderungan, bukan hukum yang kaku: tiap orang dan daerah bisa berbeda, dan nada turun-naik sangat sering dipakai dalam bahasa Inggris British.

blocks.text: Practise *Really* three ways in front of a mirror: surprised (eyes wide, the voice jumps high), doubtful (slow, down and then up) and bored (flat). Exaggerate: while you practise, too much melody is better than too little.

id.text: Latih *Really* dengan tiga cara di depan cermin: terkejut (mata melebar, suara melompat tinggi), ragu (pelan, turun lalu naik) dan bosan (datar). Lebih-lebihkan: selama latihan, melodi yang terlalu banyak lebih baik daripada terlalu sedikit.

blocks.prompt: Sari hears that her team has won an award. She had no idea. How does she say 'Really?'
options: Fast, with a big jump up ↗
blocks.explain: She's surprised and happy, so her voice jumps fast from low to very high ↗. Slow and down-up ↘↗ would sound doubtful, as if she doesn't believe it; flat and low sounds bored.

id.prompt: Sari mendengar timnya memenangkan penghargaan. Dia sama sekali tidak tahu sebelumnya. Bagaimana dia mengucapkan 'Really?'
id.explain: Dia terkejut dan senang, jadi suaranya melompat cepat dari rendah ke sangat tinggi ↗. Pelan dan turun-naik ↘↗ terdengar ragu, seolah dia tidak percaya; datar dan rendah terdengar bosan.

id.title: Ragu atau terkejut? Kata sama, nada beda

blocks.text:
In English, a lot of politeness is in the **melody**, not only in the words.

- **Requests** (asking someone to do something): *Could you send me the file? ↗* *Can you help me with this? ↗* Start fairly **high** and let the voice **rise gently** at the end. It sounds friendly and leaves the other person room to say no.
- **Offers** (offering something): *Would you like some tea? ↗* *Can I get you anything? ↗* The same gentle rise sounds warm and sincere.
- A **low, flat** voice with a **quick fall** at the end (*Could you send me the file. ↘*) can sound **impatient**, like an **order**, even with *could you* and *please*.

What about wh-questions? They still usually go down ↘ (*What would you like to drink? ↘*), but start higher and fall gently, not sharply.

**The Indonesian trap:** in Indonesian, politeness lives mostly in the words: *tolong, mohon, Pak/Bu*, and a soft *ya* at the end (*Kirim filenya ya*). So learners add *please* and keep the voice flat. In English, a flat melody can cancel the polite words. The gentle rise does the job of that friendly *ya*.

**A note on sarcasm** (saying the opposite of what you mean): *Great. ↘ Another meeting.* or *Thanks a lot. ↘* in a flat, low voice means you're annoyed, not grateful. Recognise it, but avoid it at work, especially with people you don't know well. And it doesn't work in writing: in an email, *Thanks a lot* can be read as sincere or as sarcastic.

id.text:
Dalam bahasa Inggris, sebagian besar kesopanan ada di **melodi**, bukan hanya di kata-katanya.

- **Permintaan** (meminta orang melakukan sesuatu): *Could you send me the file? ↗* *Can you help me with this? ↗* Mulai agak **tinggi** dan biarkan suaranya **naik pelan** di akhir. Terdengar ramah dan memberi ruang bagi orang itu untuk menolak.
- **Tawaran** (menawarkan sesuatu): *Would you like some tea? ↗* *Can I get you anything? ↗* Naik pelan yang sama terdengar hangat dan tulus.
- Suara yang **rendah dan datar** dengan **turun cepat** di akhir (*Could you send me the file. ↘*) bisa terdengar **tidak sabar**, seperti **perintah**, walaupun pakai *could you* dan *please*.

Bagaimana dengan wh-question? Biasanya tetap turun ↘ (*What would you like to drink? ↘*), tapi mulai lebih tinggi dan turunnya lembut, tidak tajam.

**Jebakan untuk orang Indonesia:** dalam bahasa Indonesia, kesopanan kebanyakan ada di kata-kata: *tolong, mohon, Pak/Bu*, dan *ya* yang lembut di akhir (*Kirim filenya ya*). Jadi banyak pelajar menambah *please* tapi suaranya tetap datar. Dalam bahasa Inggris, melodi yang datar bisa membatalkan kata-kata sopan itu. Naik yang pelan menggantikan tugas *ya* yang ramah itu.

**Catatan tentang sarkasme** (sindiran: mengucapkan kebalikan dari maksudmu): *Great. ↘ Another meeting.* atau *Thanks a lot. ↘* dengan suara datar dan rendah artinya kamu kesal, bukan berterima kasih. Kenali, tapi hindari di tempat kerja, apalagi dengan orang yang belum kamu kenal baik. Dan sarkasme tidak bekerja dalam tulisan: di email, *Thanks a lot* bisa dibaca tulus atau menyindir.

blocks.prompt: Rina asks a new colleague to sign a form. Which way of asking sounds most friendly?
options: Could you sign this for me? (low and flat, quick fall ↘)
Could you sign this for me? (starts higher, gentle rise ↗)
blocks.explain: Polite words plus a voice that starts higher and rises gently ↗ sound friendly. The same words low and flat with a quick fall can sound impatient, and Sign this for me said flat sounds like an order.

id.prompt: Rina meminta rekan kerja baru menandatangani formulir. Cara bertanya mana yang paling ramah?
id.explain: Kata-kata sopan ditambah suara yang mulai lebih tinggi dan naik pelan ↗ terdengar ramah. Kata-kata yang sama dengan suara rendah, datar dan turun cepat bisa terdengar tidak sabar, dan Sign this for me yang diucapkan datar terdengar seperti perintah.

blocks.text:
Recap: in a normal sentence the **content words** (nouns, main verbs, adjectives) are strong, and the strongest of all is usually the **last** one: *The MEET-ing's on THURS-day.*

When you **correct** someone or **compare** two things, you move the strongest stress to the word that is **different**, and keep the rest low and quick. This is **contrastive stress** (tekanan kontras):
- *Is the meeting on Thursday?* → *No, I said **TUES**day, not **THURS**day.*
- Someone picks up your bag → *Hey, that's **MY** bag, not **YOURS**!*
- *Did you order two coffees?* → *No, **THREE** coffees.*

**What seems to break the rule:** you learnt that small words like *my, your, I, she, not, did* are weak. In a contrast they become **strong**, because they carry the difference: *It's MY bag* (not yours), *I paid* (not Budi).

The stress goes on the word's normal stressed syllable: *TUES-day*, *ba-NA-na*, *BAN-dung*.

**Move the stress, change the meaning.** The same words can send different messages; the stressed word is the part being corrected, and everything else stays true (see the examples below).

**The Indonesian trap:** Indonesian often shows contrast with **words**: *bukan … tapi …*, *yang* (*Saya **yang** bayar*), *-lah*, *kok*. English mostly uses the **voice**. *Saya yang bayar makan siangnya* → *I paid for lunch*, with a strong *I*. If you say an English correction flat, with every word equal, the listener misses the correction.

id.text:
Ulasan: dalam kalimat biasa, **kata isi** (kata benda, kata kerja utama, kata sifat) itu kuat, dan yang paling kuat biasanya yang **terakhir**: *The MEET-ing's on THURS-day.*

Saat kamu **mengoreksi** orang atau **membandingkan** dua hal, pindahkan tekanan terkuat ke kata yang **berbeda**, dan sisanya tetap rendah dan cepat. Ini disebut **contrastive stress** (tekanan kontras):
- *Is the meeting on Thursday?* → *No, I said **TUES**day, not **THURS**day.*
- Ada orang mengambil tasmu → *Hey, that's **MY** bag, not **YOURS**!*
- *Did you order two coffees?* → *No, **THREE** coffees.*

**Yang kelihatannya melanggar aturan:** kamu sudah belajar bahwa kata kecil seperti *my, your, I, she, not, did* itu lemah. Dalam kontras, kata-kata itu jadi **kuat**, karena kata itulah yang membawa perbedaannya: *It's MY bag* (bukan punyamu), *I paid* (bukan Budi).

Tekanannya jatuh di suku kata yang biasa ditekan pada kata itu: *TUES-day*, *ba-NA-na*, *BAN-dung*.

**Pindahkan tekanannya, artinya berubah.** Kata-kata yang sama bisa membawa pesan yang berbeda; kata yang ditekan adalah bagian yang dikoreksi, dan sisanya tetap benar (lihat contoh di bawah).

**Jebakan untuk orang Indonesia:** bahasa Indonesia sering menunjukkan kontras dengan **kata**: *bukan … tapi …*, *yang* (*Saya **yang** bayar*), *-lah*, *kok*. Bahasa Inggris kebanyakan memakai **suara**. *Saya yang bayar makan siangnya* → *I paid for lunch*, dengan *I* yang kuat. Kalau kamu mengucapkan koreksi dalam bahasa Inggris dengan datar, semua kata sama kuatnya, pendengar tidak menangkap koreksinya.

blocks.text: Correct politely: a strong contrast word plus a friendly voice. *Sorry, I think it's on TUESday.* With a hard, flat voice the same stress can sound annoyed.

id.text: Koreksi dengan sopan: satu kata kontras yang kuat ditambah suara yang ramah. *Sorry, I think it's on TUESday.* Dengan suara yang keras dan datar, tekanan yang sama bisa terdengar kesal.

blocks.prompt: Pak Hasan asks: 'Is the new client from Bandung?' She's from Bogor. In the answer 'No, she's from Bogor', which word gets the strongest stress?
blocks.explain: Bogor is the word that corrects Bandung, so it gets the strongest stress: *No, she's from BO-gor.* she's and from stay weak, because nothing about them is being corrected.

id.prompt: Pak Hasan bertanya: 'Is the new client from Bandung?' Kliennya dari Bogor. Dalam jawaban 'No, she's from Bogor', kata mana yang mendapat tekanan paling kuat?
id.explain: Bogor adalah kata yang mengoreksi Bandung, jadi kata itu mendapat tekanan paling kuat: *No, she's from BO-gor.* she's dan from tetap lemah, karena tidak ada yang dikoreksi pada kata-kata itu.

material.title: Chunks and pauses when you present

blocks.text:
When you present (a team meeting, a pitch, a thesis defence), your listeners can't read your mind or your slide as fast as you speak. Help them by speaking in **chunks**. A **chunk** (also called a **thought group**) is a group of words that belong together, said as one unit, with a short **pause** after it. In a script we mark the pause with **|**:
*Last year | our sales | rose by ten percent.*

**Where to pause:**
- at a comma or full stop;
- after a time or place phrase at the start: *In the first quarter |*, *In Surabaya |*;
- after a long subject: *Our two new branches in Medan | opened in May.*
- before linking words: *| but*, *| because*, *| so*.

**Where NOT to pause:** inside a group that belongs together: *the | report* ✗, *in | Bandung* ✗, *ten | percent* ✗, *our | sales* ✗.

**Inside each chunk**, one word gets the main stress, usually the last content word: *Last YEAR | our SALES | rose by ten PER-cent.* At the end of a chunk the voice often stays up or level ('more is coming'), and it falls ↘ at the end of the sentence, just like a list.

**The Indonesian trap (and the common error):** reading the slide in **one long breath**, fast, because you're nervous, or pausing only when you run out of air, in the middle of a group: *our sales in | Surabaya*. Another habit: filling every pause with *eee…*. In English a short **silent** pause sounds calm and confident. Slow down a little for numbers and key points.

Long sentences can often be chunked in more than one good way. What matters: never split a group, and give your listeners time.

id.text:
Saat kamu presentasi (rapat tim, pitching, sidang skripsi), pendengarmu tidak bisa membaca pikiranmu atau slide-mu secepat kamu berbicara. Bantu mereka dengan berbicara dalam **potongan** (chunk). **Chunk** (disebut juga **thought group**) adalah sekelompok kata yang satu kesatuan, diucapkan sebagai satu unit, dengan **jeda** singkat setelahnya. Di naskah, jedanya kita tandai dengan **|**:
*Last year | our sales | rose by ten percent.*

**Di mana memberi jeda:**
- di tanda koma atau titik;
- setelah keterangan waktu atau tempat di awal kalimat: *In the first quarter |*, *In Surabaya |*;
- setelah subjek yang panjang (subjek = siapa atau apa yang dibicarakan): *Our two new branches in Medan | opened in May.*
- sebelum kata penghubung: *| but*, *| because*, *| so*.

**Di mana TIDAK boleh berhenti:** di tengah kelompok kata yang satu kesatuan: *the | report* ✗, *in | Bandung* ✗, *ten | percent* ✗, *our | sales* ✗.

**Di dalam setiap potongan**, satu kata mendapat tekanan utama, biasanya kata isi yang terakhir: *Last YEAR | our SALES | rose by ten PER-cent.* Di akhir potongan, suara sering tetap di atas atau datar ('masih ada lanjutannya'), dan turun ↘ di akhir kalimat, persis seperti daftar.

**Jebakan untuk orang Indonesia (dan kesalahan yang umum):** membaca slide dalam **satu tarikan napas panjang**, cepat, karena gugup, atau berhenti hanya saat kehabisan napas, di tengah kelompok kata: *our sales in | Surabaya*. Kebiasaan lain: mengisi setiap jeda dengan *eee…*. Dalam bahasa Inggris, jeda **diam** yang singkat terdengar tenang dan percaya diri. Pelankan sedikit untuk angka dan poin penting.

Kalimat yang panjang sering bisa dipotong dengan lebih dari satu cara yang baik. Yang penting: jangan pernah memecah satu kelompok kata, dan beri pendengarmu waktu.

blocks.text: Prepare your script: print it, mark every pause with |, and underline the main word in each chunk. Read it aloud slowly, pausing in silence at each |. When you watch good speakers (for example TED talks), notice where they pause.

id.text: Siapkan naskahmu: cetak, tandai setiap jeda dengan |, dan garis bawahi kata utama di setiap potongan. Baca dengan suara keras pelan-pelan, diam sebentar di setiap |. Saat menonton pembicara yang bagus (misalnya TED talks), perhatikan di mana mereka memberi jeda.

blocks.prompt: Which sentence has a pause in the wrong place?
options: In Bandung | we opened two stores.
We opened two | stores in Bandung.
We opened two stores | in Bandung.
blocks.explain: two | stores splits a number from its word, and they belong together. A pause after the place phrase at the start (In Bandung |) is natural, and a short pause before in Bandung at the end is fine too.

id.prompt: Kalimat mana yang jedanya di tempat yang salah?
id.explain: two | stores memisahkan angka dari katanya, padahal keduanya satu kelompok. Jeda setelah keterangan tempat di awal (In Bandung |) terdengar alami, dan jeda singkat sebelum in Bandung di akhir juga tidak apa-apa.

id.intro: Kamu sudah bisa menaikkan ↗ dan menurunkan ↘ suara untuk daftar, question tag dan perasaan. Sekarang kamu memakainya di dunia kerja: untuk terdengar ragu, terkejut atau sopan, untuk mengoreksi orang dengan satu kata yang ditekan kuat (I said TUESday, not THURSday), dan untuk presentasi dalam potongan-potongan yang jelas dengan jeda singkat. Rekamannya dibaca dengan suara yang tenang dan alami, jadi melodinya kamu yang tambahkan: ucapkan setiap contoh dengan suara keras dan sedikit dilebih-lebihkan.

assessment.ia-1: Di sebuah rapat, Budi bilang: 'The new app will be ready next week.' Bu Ani menjawab 'Really…?' dengan pelan, dan suaranya turun lalu naik lagi ↘↗. Bagaimana perasaannya tentang kabar dari Budi? Tulis surprised, doubtful atau bored.
assessment.ia-2: Sari meminta tolong rekan kerjanya: 'Could you check my slides before the meeting?' Dia mengucapkannya dengan suara rendah dan datar yang turun cepat di akhir. Bagaimana kedengarannya bagi rekannya? Tulis friendly atau impatient.
assessment.ia-3: Budi bilang: 'I didn't say Rina LOST the files.' (LOST diucapkan dengan tekanan ekstra.) Apa maksudnya? Tulis A, B atau C. A: Someone else lost the files, not Rina. B: Rina did something else with the files, for example she deleted them. C: Someone else said it, not Budi.
assessment.ia-4: Pak Hasan mengira Dimas yang mengirim laporan penjualan ke klien. Sebenarnya Sari yang mengirimnya. Sari bilang kepadanya: 'I sent the report.' Kata mana yang paling dia tekan? Tulis katanya dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.ia-5: Dengarkan pertanyaan Rina. Pelatihannya ada di ruang dua belas di lantai tiga. Kamu menjawab: 'No, it's in room twelve on the third floor.' Satu kata mana yang paling kamu tekan? Tulis katanya dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.ia-6: Seorang presenter punya tiga versi kalimat slide yang sama, dengan | sebagai tanda jeda. Mana yang dipotong dengan jelas? Tulis A, B atau C. A: This year our | team in Bandung doubled | its sales. B: This year | our team in Bandung | doubled its sales. C: This | year our team | in Bandung doubled its | sales.
assessment.ia-7: Dimas ingin memberi satu jeda singkat di kalimat slide-nya ini: 'In the second half of the year our team opened three new offices.' Setelah kata apa tempat terbaik untuk jedanya? Tulis katanya dalam bahasa Inggris.
